content: The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) evaluated whether conflicts of interest among experts involved in the development of recommendations for drug treatment of severe hypertension in pregnancy were significant enough to compromise the objectivity of the guideline development process. To ensure consistency, the Steering Group applied the criteria outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development to assess the severity of conflicts of interest for all participating experts. Findings from the Declaration of Interest (DOI) statements were managed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with WHO DOI guidelines and communicated to the experts. If a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant and unlikely to affect the credibility of the guideline development process, the experts were only required to disclose such conflicts openly at the beginning of the GDG meeting, with no further actions taken. Annex 3 provides a summary of the DOI statements and the management of declared conflicts by the Steering Group. During the GDG meeting, the group reviewed and discussed the evidence summary and sought clarifications. In addition to evaluating the balance between the desirable and undesirable effects of the intervention and the overall certainty of the evidence, the GDG applied additional criteria from the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework to determine the direction and strength of the recommendations. These criteria included stakeholders’ values, resource implications, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. The group’s considerations were informed by their expertise and supported by evidence from literature searches where available. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the participants. None of the GDG members opposed the recommendations. Before the online meeting, the WHO Steering Group prepared draft versions of the GRADE evidence profiles, evidence summaries, and other relevant documents for the GDG’s deliberations. These drafts were shared with meeting participants two weeks in advance for their comments. During the meeting, the documents were revised based on participants’ deliberations and remarks. After the meeting, the WHO Steering Group drafted a recommendation document to accurately reflect the discussions and decisions of the participants. This draft was sent electronically to GDG members and the External Review Group for final review and approval. Following review and approval by the GDG and the External Review Group, the final document was sent to eight external independent experts who were not involved in the guideline panel for peer review. The WHO Steering Group evaluated the peer reviewers’ inputs for inclusion in the document. Post-meeting and external peer review, the WHO Steering Group made only factual corrections and language improvements to enhance clarity. The GDG adopted recommendations for the drug treatment of severe hypertension in pregnancy. Evidence on the effectiveness of the intervention was derived from a systematic review and summarized in GRADE tables (Annex 5). The certainty of the supporting evidence was rated as very low for most critical outcomes. To ensure proper understanding and implementation of the recommendations, additional remarks summarizing the GDG’s discussions are included under each recommendation. 1. Women with severe hypertension during pregnancy should receive treatment with antihypertensive drugs (strong recommendation, very low certainty evidence). The GDG agreed that there is no clinical uncertainty regarding the benefits of treating severe hypertension during pregnancy. This recommendation was based on expert opinion, as most maternal deaths related to hypertensive disorders are associated with complications of uncontrolled severe high blood pressure. The group concluded that antihypertensive treatment should be recommended in all cases of severe hypertension. 2. The choice and route of administration of an antihypertensive drug for severe hypertension during pregnancy should primarily depend on the prescribing clinician’s experience with the drug, its cost, and local availability (conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence). The GDG noted that the evidence base for this recommendation is limited and that some antihypertensive drugs may not be feasible options in many settings. Hydralazine, alpha methyldopa, beta blockers (including labetalol), and nifedipine have been extensively used and are considered reasonable choices until further evidence becomes available. The group also noted no evidence suggesting adverse interactions between nifedipine and magnesium sulfate. The use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and sodium nitroprusside should be avoided due to safety concerns. The dissemination and implementation of these recommendations require the involvement of all stakeholders and organizations providing care for pregnant women at international, national, and local levels. It is essential to increase access and strengthen the capacity of health centers to deliver high-quality services to all women giving birth. These recommendations should be integrated into antenatal and intrapartum care packages and programs at country and health-facility levels where appropriate. A shorter document summarizing the recommendations, remarks, implementation considerations, and research priorities will be developed for public dissemination. This document will include annexes containing detailed information, such as methods, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and GRADE tables. The recommendations will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. They will also be available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during meetings or scientific conferences attended by relevant WHO staff. The recommendations document will be translated into the six UN languages and disseminated through WHO regional offices. Technical assistance will be provided to any WHO regional office willing to translate the full recommendations into these languages. Successful implementation of these recommendations into national programs and healthcare services depends on well-planned, participatory, consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. This may include developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols. The recommendations should be adapted into locally appropriate documents to meet the specific needs of each country and health service, with any changes made transparently. Interventions should be established to create an enabling environment for the use of these recommendations, including ensuring the availability of antihypertensive drugs and promoting evidence-based practices among healthcare providers. Local professional societies play a crucial role, and an inclusive, participatory process should be encouraged. Healthcare providers should discuss risks, benefits, and treatment options with women to facilitate informed decision-making. Guidance on managing severe hypertension in pregnancy, including doses and routes of administration, is available in the WHO handbook Managing complications of pregnancy and childbirth (Second edition). The GDG identified critical knowledge gaps that need to be addressed through primary research, which may impact these recommendations. High-priority research areas include: The relative effectiveness of available drugs for severe acute hypertension, including effects on the fetus and newborn. Understanding the relative importance women with hypertension during pregnancy place on health outcomes and their preferences regarding treatment options. Evaluating interventions that enable women to manage their own blood pressure during pregnancy (e.g., diet, exercise, and other interventions). Managing severe hypertension in pregnancy at primary and secondary care levels (prior to referral to higher-level facilities) in low-resource settings. Evaluating health education interventions for communicating with women experiencing hypertension during pregnancy. Implementing these evidence-based recommendations will require resources to ensure safe implementation, including staff time for monitoring women undergoing drug treatment for severe hypertension in pregnancy. Updating training curricula and providing training will enhance impact and facilitate implementation. Standardizing care by incorporating recommendations into existing maternity care packages and protocols can encourage behavior change among healthcare providers. Implementation should be monitored at the health-service level as part of broader efforts to improve the quality of maternal and newborn care. Methods such as interrupted time series, clinical audits, or criterion-based clinical audits can be used to collect relevant data. Clearly defined review criteria and indicators are needed and should align with locally agreed targets. These can be aligned with the standards and indicators described in the WHO document Standards for improving quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) regularly reviews WHO’s portfolio of maternal and perinatal health recommendations and advises on prioritizing new and existing questions for recommendation development and updating. These recommendations will be reviewed and prioritized by the Executive GSG. If new evidence that could impact the current evidence base is identified, the recommendations may be updated. If no new reports or information are identified, the recommendations may be revalidated. Following publication and dissemination of the updated recommendations, any concerns about their validity will be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans to update the recommendations. WHO welcomes suggestions regarding additional questions for inclusion in the updated recommendations.
